channel.title: doyouknow.app - English
channel.description: Surprising facts about UAE, Saudi Arabia, and the world.

item.title: How a Barcode Scanner Actually Reads Black and White Lines
item.description: A barcode scanner isn't reading lines at all. It is timing the precise widths of bars and spaces, then converting those measured distances into digits.

item.title: How a Camera Obscura Actually Projects an Image With No Lens
item.description: A dark room with one small hole can project a real, detailed image of the outside world. No lens, no glass, no electronics — just straight lines of light.

item.title: How a Cochlear Implant Actually Lets Deaf People Hear
item.description: A cochlear implant does not amplify sound like a hearing aid. It bypasses the damaged inner ear entirely and sends electrical signals straight to the auditory nerve.

item.title: How a Hovercraft Actually Floats on a Cushion of Air
item.description: A hovercraft never displaces water like a boat. It continuously pumps a cushion of pressurized air beneath itself, which is why it can glide over land, ice, and mud too.

item.title: How a Lock and Key Actually Decide Which Shape Fits
item.description: A key is really just a physical record of pin heights. Every wrong key leaves one pin misaligned, and that single pin is enough to stop the whole lock.

item.title: How a Metal Detector Actually Finds Buried Treasure
item.description: A metal detector never actually senses metal directly. It generates its own magnetic field and listens for the tiny electrical echo that field creates in anything metallic nearby.

item.title: How a Thermostat Actually Decides When to Turn Your HVAC On
item.description: A thermostat never switches equipment at one exact temperature. A deliberate gap called the deadband, plus minimum cycle timers, protect the compressor from wearing itself out.

item.title: How Braille Actually Lets Fingertips Read Text
item.description: Braille packs every letter and number into a six-dot cell, a design borrowed from a night-reading military code and simplified until fingertips read it as fast as eyes scan print.

item.title: How Camera Shutter Speed Actually Freezes or Blurs Motion
item.description: Shutter speed is just a measurement of time, but that single number decides whether a hummingbird's wings freeze sharp or blur into a soft smear.

item.title: How EMV Chip Cards Actually Stop Counterfeit Fraud
item.description: EMV chip cards generate a brand-new one-time cryptographic code for every transaction, using a secret key locked inside tamper-resistant silicon that a stolen card cannot expose.

item.title: How Glass Blowing Actually Shapes Molten Glass With Breath
item.description: Glass at the right temperature behaves like thick honey, not liquid or solid. That narrow window is the only reason a human breath can shape it into a vase.

item.title: How Morse Code Actually Packs an Alphabet Into Dots and Dashes
item.description: The letter E is one dot because it is the most common letter in English. Morse code's design quietly anticipated modern data compression a century before computers existed.

item.title: How Septic Tanks Actually Treat Wastewater Without a Sewer Line
item.description: A septic tank separates solids from wastewater using gravity and bacteria, then relies on a drain field to filter the remaining liquid through soil before it reaches groundwater.

item.title: How Suspension Bridges Actually Hold Up Their Own Weight
item.description: Suspension bridges hang their deck from cables in pure tension, letting steel do what it does best — spanning distances no beam or truss bridge could ever match.

item.title: How the Antikythera Mechanism Actually Predicted the Sky
item.description: A corroded bronze shipwreck find turned out to be a 2,000-year-old hand-cranked mechanical computer that used precision gears to predict eclipses and track the moon.

item.title: How the Panama Canal Locks Actually Lift Ships Over a Mountain
item.description: The Panama Canal has no pumps lifting ships. Gravity-fed water from an artificial lake raises and lowers vessels through concrete chambers, now strained by drought.

item.title: How Wind Turbines Actually Generate Electricity
item.description: Wind turbines capture kinetic energy from moving air through airplane-wing-shaped blades, spinning a generator through a gearbox to produce grid-ready electricity.

item.title: Why the Ozone Layer Is Actually Recovering
item.description: A global ban on ozone-destroying chemicals, agreed by every country on Earth through the Montreal Protocol, has the ozone layer on track to fully recover by around 2066.

item.title: Why the QWERTY Keyboard Layout Actually Won
item.description: QWERTY was designed to stop mechanical typewriter jams, not to slow typists down — once trained typists and makers locked in around it, no faster layout could dislodge it.

item.title: Why Wisdom Teeth Actually Need to Come Out
item.description: Modern jaws are usually too small for a third set of molars evolved for a tougher ancestral diet, which is why impacted wisdom teeth so often need surgical removal.
